item.title: Digital Forensics: Fixing a Corrupted Disk After File Exfiltration
item.description:
Corrupted MBR used to obstruct investigation into insider data exfiltration. NTFS artifacts including $MFT and $UsnJrnl expose the full attack chain despite deliberate anti-forensic wiping.
Key findings:
- The MBR's final two bytes (boot signature 0x55 0xAA) were overwritten to prevent tools like Autopsy and FTK Imager from reading the image. Repair requires a hex editor such as HxD: overwrite, never delete, those bytes to restore the signature before any further analysis.
- After repair, export and parse MFT with MFTECmd.exe (Eric Zimmerman's EZTools): MFTECmd.exe -f ..\Evidence$MFT --csv ..\Evidence\ --csvf MFT.csv. Even deleted file records survive here, revealing Excel sheets, PDFs, and zip archives flagged as sensitive corporate data.
- $UsnJrnl (J) logged the full exfiltration sequence: a folder named "data Exfil" was created, files were appended to "New Compressed (zipped) Folder.zip", then renamed and deleted. Parse J with MFTECmd, open in Timeline Explorer, and filter Update Reason to FileDelete.
- DiskWipe.exe was found on the second partition. To confirm execution and tie actions to a user, extend the investigation into Prefetch, Shellbags, registry, and NTUSER.DAT.
Always hash-verify the forensic image before touching it, then work only on a verified copy. MFT and $UsnJrnl together reconstruct what wipers try to erase.

item.title: PEEP: A Browser RAT Posing as a Chrome Extension
item.description:
PEEP, a RedExt-derived browser RAT disguised as "Smart Bookmarks," converts Chrome and Edge into persistent backdoors with host-level command execution, session theft, and file access, all over plaintext HTTP.
Key findings:
- PEEP is a post-exploitation toolkit requiring prior admin or code execution access. Its PowerShell installers (install_silent.ps1, patch_secure_prefs.ps1) forge Chromium's Secure Preferences HMAC-SHA256 integrity values (protection.macs and super_mac) so the sideloaded extension passes the browser's own integrity check and silently re-enables at every launch (T1553). Four layered persistence mechanisms, Secure Preferences forgery, enterprise ExtensionInstallForcelist policy, external sideloading, and a ScriptCache "Ghost Anchor" fallback, mean no single cleanup action removes all of it.
- The native-messaging host com.peep.lab (nm_host.exe, a 37.7 MB unsigned Node.js pkg binary) bridges the browser sandbox to the OS, supporting NM_SHELL (cmd/PowerShell/bash), filesystem read/write/delete, process listing, and service enumeration. The agent beacons every 30 seconds over plaintext HTTP to 206.237.30[.]232 (AS55933, Cloudie, Hong Kong) with X-PEEP-Agent-Key and X-PEEP-Agent-Id headers, auto-exfiltrating cookies, history, and open tabs to /api/exfil.

item.title: DPRK APTs: Ted backdoor and curlRAT target South Korean media and automotive sectors
item.description:
DPRK APTs deploy "ted backdoor" and curlRAT against South Korean 🇰🇷 automotive and media sectors, embedding a custom plugin directly into HAProxy 2.8.12 for stealthy long-term espionage dating to early 2025.
- Ted backdoor is compiled into the victim's own HAProxy 2.8.12 build (72e70936f0dbe459142a1d867617c35f8d0cce5d18c6a49e1090a2a5adc8e558, 18MB) as ted_plugin, hooking the native HTTP filter API to intercept SSL-decrypted traffic, harvest session cookies, and inject payloads into responses for selected IPs, all while legitimate load-balancing continues. C2 requests masquerade as fetches for /favorite_list_2x_m500_ico.jpg and HAProxy connection counters are atomically scrubbed (T1562.006) so the connection never appears in backend logs.
- CurlRAT hides inside trojanized crond, agetty, atd, and polkitd binaries. The stager (5db1b6d52faf60b4f32d6fd0c7c938e4d05d29a14c32ded4a9668357c08b6a91) overwrites the legitimate crond binary, timestomps it to match /usr/bin/ssh (T1070.006), then erases traces from bash_history, audit.log, auth.log, and syslog via /tmp/jasper-log (T1070.002). CurlRAT supports six C2 modes including reverse shell, PTY shell, and staged payload drop, polling img.darklights[.]store and img.monderhouse[.]space over HTTPS with a feedback XOR plus Base64 cipher and a 12-hour default poll interval.

item.title: Chinese Hackers Use AI Agents in Multi-Country Cyber Campaign
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 actors deploy the SecFlow AI orchestration framework across five countries, using Claude, Qwen, and DeepSeek to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, and credential theft against government and industrial targets.
- Five accidentally exposed open directories let Hunt.io reconstruct the entire SecFlow operation from the inside. The framework split tasks across AI "workers" (reconnaissance, exploitation, collection, reporting) and routed model requests through private proxies tied to niestools[.]com, avoiding official APIs and attribution.
- The deepest confirmed breach hit a Fengtai District government OA environment: ASPX webshells provided persistent access, LSASS was dumped in 37 chunks via an authenticated SOCKS route to evade size-based detection, and SAM/SYSTEM hives were pulled. 822 user records, 949 attachments (1.28 GB), and patient health data were exfiltrated.
- The webshell toolkit, named GLUTTON by the operators, hid payloads inside PNG files using steganography. Code was XOR-encrypted and embedded in RGB channel data, then decoded and loaded directly into memory server-side. File-extension or content-type controls will not catch this.
- A fake MySQL deserialization service flipped initial access: it accepted connections from vulnerable Java clients and returned crafted responses to trigger remote code execution on the connecting host, turning an outbound database query into inbound execution.

item.title: Attacking and Defending SCOM: Management Server Relay and Obtaining Run As Credentials
item.description:
Default SCOM deployments hand attackers a path from standard domain user to code execution on every monitored host, including domain controllers, via NTLM relay and DPAPI credential dumping.
Key findings:
- The relay attack targets the MSOMSdkSvc/ SPN sitting on the Management Server computer account by default. Using PetitPotam to coerce authentication and impacket-ntlmrelayx to relay it, an attacker inserts their SID into the AzMan_Role_SIDMember table in the OperationsManager database, granting Operations Console access from a standard domain account. SCOMHunter automates the enumeration and relay query.
- Once in the Operations Console, attackers create Agent Tasks targeting any monitored host, including domain controllers, running as SYSTEM. A single task like "cmd.exe /c net group Domain Admins domainuser /add /domain" completes the escalation.
- Run As credentials are stored as DPAPI-protected blobs in the registry under the HealthService key on every monitored host. SCOMHunter's DPAPI module pulls these over SMB, retrieves the MasterKey via LSA secrets, and decrypts them. Accounts set to Less secure distribution land on every agent automatically.
Fix: Move the MSOMSdkSvc/ SPN off the Management Server computer account onto a gMSA using setspn. Set all Run As accounts to More secure distribution. Disable the web console PowerShell widget.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2095830154744418732

item.title: Angry Birds: Toy Ghouls’ new toys
item.description:
Toy Ghouls deploys two custom backdoors using MQTT and Matrix as C2 channels against Russian 🇷🇺 organizations, marking a shift from public tools toward purpose-built tradecraft.
Key findings:
- Delivered via WinRM using Evil-WinRM and WinRM-fs, the backdoors (cplsupport.exe and wtass.exe) install as Windows services named "Problem Reports Control Panel" and "Windows Telemetry Aggregator Service." Config is sealed using ChaCha20-Poly1305 keyed to HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid, binding it to the victim machine after first run.
- The HiveMQ version C2s through broker.hivemq.com and executes commands via PowerShell.exe with -NonInteractive -NoProfile -Command in hidden mode. The Element version uses meet.element[.]tw on the Matrix protocol; commands prefix with cmd: and operator account is named panel-bot, recoverable from Element's SQLite databases on disk.
- Both versions beacon system status and metrics (CPU, memory, disk) at configurable intervals and call http://ip-api.com/json on startup for geolocation, a useful first-beacon artifact in proxy or firewall logs.
- IOCs: MD5 BFADBEEE63A4F0BF19EC9DEB8FA58F58 (cplsupport.exe), 7916C33688385525078BEE504C90F359 (wtass.exe). Registry: HKLM\Software\synapse\Config\SealedConfig, HKLM\Software\SynapseAgent\metrics_interval.
Hunt for outbound TLS to broker.hivemq.com port 8883 and meet.element[.]tw from non-browser processes, plus PowerShell children of service host processes.

item.title: Coder's registry infrastructure compromised to push malicious modules
item.description:
Coder's Cloudflare registry hijacked on Aug 31 to push credential-stealing Terraform modules to developers at Dropbox, Palantir, the US 🇺🇸 government, and defense contractors.
- Attacker gained access to Coder's Cloudflare infrastructure and injected unauthorized IP addresses into the registry.coder.com server pool. Between 07:35 and 21:45 UTC on August 31, Cloudflare routed a subset of module requests to attacker-controlled servers serving trojanized Terraform modules.
- The malicious modules acted as infostealers, harvesting provisioner env vars, cloud and AI API keys, CI/CD credentials, SSH keys, OIDC tokens, terminal history, config-file secrets, and Coder database passwords when running inside coderd.
- Exfiltration destination was the lookalike domain coder-infra[.]com. Because the attacker's infrastructure is outside Coder's control, the project cannot conclusively identify every compromised deployment.
- Patched releases are 2.37.0, 2.36.4, 2.35.7, and 2.34.9. Before upgrading, hunt firewall, proxy, DNS, and VPC flow logs for connections to coder-infra[.]com, and search provisioner logs for data.external.telemetry.
Rotate every secret class listed above immediately. Run Coder's published SQL query to identify affected cached modules and template versions, then purge them. Treat any secret exposed during the window as fully compromised.

item.title: Signature Optional - Analysis of CVE-2026-28323
item.description:
CVE-2026-28323 in SolarWinds Web Help Desk allows full session takeover via a single forged SAML POST, no credentials required. Bishop Fox confirmed end-to-end exploitation.
Key findings:
- SolarWinds Web Help Desk treated SAML signature verification as optional and skipped all remaining spec-required validation steps, meaning an attacker could forge an arbitrary SAML assertion and the application accepted it as legitimate.
- Bishop Fox confirmed the full exploit chain end to end: one crafted POST request with a forged SAML response, zero credentials, full authenticated session returned. No chained CVEs, no prior foothold needed. Exploitation is trivially reproducible.
- DFIR artifact focus: hunt your web server access logs for POST requests to the SAML assertion consumer service endpoint with malformed or unsigned SAMLResponse values, especially those resulting in HTTP 200 or redirect responses that indicate session creation.
- Scope: any SolarWinds Web Help Desk deployment with SAML SSO enabled is affected until the patch is applied. Web Help Desk is common in enterprise IT and MSP environments, making this a high-value lateral movement or initial access target.
Patch immediately. If patching is delayed, disable SAML SSO and fall back to local authentication. Review auth logs for unexpected SSO-authenticated sessions, particularly service or admin accounts. Full technical root cause and detection detail are in the Bishop Fox report.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2095664289994486209

item.title: Incident response guide for AWS CloudTrail investigations – Part 1
item.description:
AWS CloudTrail investigation playbook from AWS SIRT breaks down two real incident scenarios: cross-account S3 ransomware-style deletion and console-credential cryptomining via CloudFormation, with annotated log evidence throughout.
Key findings:
- In Scenario 1, a threat actor assumed the CrossAccountS3Access role from a trusted account, used a masquerading session name "dev-migration-script" to blend into operational noise, performed ListBuckets recon at 14:31:22Z, then executed scripted REST.COPY.OBJECT exfiltration followed by REST.DELETE.OBJECT destruction of q4-2024.xlsx, pii-database.csv, and prod-database-backup.sql within a 13-second window. The copy-then-delete sequence is the ransomware tell: data was stolen before destruction to enable extortion.
- In Scenario 2, console credentials without MFA (mfaAuthenticated: false) let a threat actor deploy a CloudFormation stack named CRYPTO in us-east-1 just 50 seconds after session creation. The userAgent field (exec-env/CloudShell) reveals they launched CloudShell to run a prepackaged script, bypassing static API key monitoring while staying inside the console trust boundary. sessionCredentialFromConsole: true is the pivot field separating console-sourced sessions from programmatic access.

item.title: Incident response guide for AWS CloudTrail investigations – Part 2
item.description:
SSRF to IMDSv1 credential theft cascades into multi-Region Amazon Bedrock misuse. AWS SIRT breaks down the full attack chain with annotated CloudTrail evidence and a response checklist.
Key findings:
- The chain started with an SSRF flaw in a web app on an EC2 instance carrying the "webdev" IAM role. Because IMDSv1 requires no session token, the attacker hit 169.254.169.254 and walked away with temporary role credentials. The CloudTrail smoking gun is ec2RoleDelivery: "1.0" in the userIdentity block. That single field confirms IMDSv1 delivery and the SSRF vector without needing application logs.
- Four events tell the whole story: a failed CreateUser for "adm1n" (typosquatting with a numeral 1) at 15:53 UTC, a no-MFA ConsoleLogin success at 15:59, a ListFoundationModels recon call in us-east-2 at 17:20, then a Converse invocation of amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 at 17:25. Same source IP 75.3.231[.]105, same webdev role session throughout.
- The Region hop from us-east-1 to us-east-2 was deliberate evasion. Inconsistent cross-Region monitoring let the Bedrock activity go initially unnoticed. sessionCredentialFromConsole: "true" in Event 3 ties the Bedrock calls back to the hijacked console session, not a fresh credential pull.
- CloudTrail records the Converse call and token counts (944 input, 126 output) but NOT prompt or response content. If Bedrock model invocation logging was not enabled, the data sent to the model cannot be recovered post-incident.

item.title: Attackers Actively Exploiting Critical Vulnerability in Super Forms Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-14894 (CVSS 9.8): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in the Super Forms WordPress plugin is actively exploited at scale, with 250,000+ blocked attempts and PHP webshells being dropped on vulnerable sites.
- CVE-2026-14894 affects Super Forms <= 6.3.313. The submit_form() nopriv AJAX handler accepts a base64-encoded datauristring, decodes it, and writes it to disk using an attacker-controlled filename with zero file-type validation. A valid nonce is freely minted via the super_create_nonce nopriv endpoint, so the full exploit chain is just two unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php.
- The webshell observed in the wild is named Mushr00w_upl.php, a browser-based uploader used to stage further payloads. Exploitation began July 14, 2026, five days after disclosure, with a major spike August 18-25. Top offending IPs include 103.168.147[.]235 (106k+ requests) and 103.168.146[.]131 (82k+ requests).
- For incident response: search the entire WordPress docroot for .php files created or modified on or after July 8, 2026. Check web server access logs for POST requests to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with action=super_submit_form. The filename Mushr00w_upl.php is a strong IOC but attackers vary filenames and can use path traversal to place shells outside the upload directory.
Patch to Super Forms 6.3.314 immediately.

item.title: Modern Adventures in Azure Privilege Escalation
item.description:
The "Anyscale Platform Administrator Role" Azure built-in role allowed unconstrained escalation to Owner-equivalent access, reported to MSRC 6/8/2026 and patched 6/22/2026.
- The Anyscale Platform Administrator Role (GUID 3e9f3756-203e-4734-a0b8-4b68691ffae3) held Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write and /delete without any ABAC Conditions. Of 28 built-in roles carrying roleAssignments/write, only 4 lacked constraining ABAC Conditions: Owner, User Access Administrator, RBAC Administrator, and this role. Any principal holding it could arbitrarily assign any role, including Owner, to any principal in scope.
- The recommended Azure Portal ABAC Condition ("Allow user to assign all roles except Owner, UAA, RBAC") can be bypassed because it constrains only roleAssignments/write and /delete, not Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/write. A constrained Owner or UAA can create a custom role with * or roleAssignments/write, then self-assign it, and the unconstrained custom role takes priority.
- The undocumented ARM API endpoint (Role Definitions List, version 2023-07-01-preview) with the hasAllPermissions filter lets you map any permission directly to every built-in and custom role that contains it, surfacing unexpected hits like Log Analytics Contributor and Virtual Machine Contributor both holding Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action.

item.title: ASCII smuggling crosses over from AI prompt injection to phishing evasion
item.description:
An AI-era evasion technique jumped from prompt injection research into high-volume phishing: invisible Unicode tag characters (U+E0000-U+E007F) spliced into financial keywords to break spam filters, peaking at 2.37 million messages per day.
Key findings:
- Starting February 9, 2026, signature hits jumped from ~21,000 to 1.3 million messages overnight. The campaign ran weekdays only, paused every weekend, peaked February 26, and dropped sharply after May 15. Finance-themed lure words like "funding" were split as fun[U+E0020]ding, defeating literal string matches and disrupting ML tokenizers without alerting recipients. MITRE T1027 / AML.T0068.
- ~150 disposable sender domains built from a recycled 28-token finance vocabulary (capital, fund, loan, loc, boost, etc.) relayed through ActiveCampaign infrastructure. Envelope senders follow the pattern em-[digits].[brand-domain]; click-tracking routes through acemlnd[.]com and activehosted[.]com. ~92% of volume originated from 173.236.20[.]0/24, a legitimate shared platform block useful for scoping, not blocking alone.
- The detection gap: pipelines that do not normalize U+E0000-U+E007F before applying signatures or ML classifiers may miss the obfuscation. OCR-based content analysis sidesteps it entirely. Exclude England/Scotland/Wales flag emojis (legitimately encoded with tag characters) before treating the range as malicious.

item.title: From ClickFix to SilentEncryptor: A Simple Yet Destructive Path to Ransomware Deployment
item.description:
StopAndProtect campaign uses ClickFix social engineering on hacked WordPress sites to deploy SilentEncryptor ransomware, active since May 2026 with 22 confirmed variants now identified.
- ClickFix is the initial access vector (T1204.002): visitors to compromised WordPress sites see a fake CAPTCHA prompt that instructs them to copy and run a PowerShell command, handing the attacker execution without any exploit.
- SilentEncryptor pulls its target list and ransom note dynamically from C2, meaning the attacker controls which endpoints get encrypted and can rotate messaging between victims. Three original samples share the embedded marker string "*V*RrETTY" and base64-encoded wallet paths covering Bitcoin, Ethereum, Exodus, Dash, Dogecoin, and others under AppData\Roaming.
- A suspected OPSEC failure caused the threat actor to upload their own desktop files to C2, giving researchers rare visibility into the operation's infrastructure, all hosted on the same pool of vulnerable WordPress sites.
- Stairwell's YARA rule scanned their malware corpus and surfaced 22 variants beyond the original three, with sample hashes including 65550f6d0ffec8421f703cdc7273d9c0563b3d480fe6702bad294a18afe72143 and a5b512c09a6b0add18397238d0c64ff34b6d95f4114efe808df03e3e11c29fb1.
Deploy the YARA rule retroactively across your environment and hunt for PowerShell processes spawned from browser or clipboard activity. Full IOC list and YARA rule are in the report.

item.title: AI-Generated BEC Phishing from a Compromised Mailbox | Invictus Incident Response
item.description:
AI-polished BEC arrives from a legitimately compromised mailbox, bypassing reputation filters. A two-stage redirect chain (AWS S3 to Cloudflare-fronted domain) ends in an AiTM Google credential harvester.
Key findings:
- The lure originated from a real grocery retailer's compromised mailbox, subject "Urgent Review Required - Purchase Order and Invoice Discrepancies." No lookalike domain, no spoof signal for gateways to catch. Body assessed as LLM-generated: structurally flawless, generically polite, missing the specific PO numbers a real dispute would include (T1199, T1078.004).
- Redirect chain: projectorg878990.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws[.]com/index.html poses as an "RFP Access Portal," then bounces to purchasesord[.]com (Cloudflare-fronted, first seen 25 Aug 2026), which serves a Google sign-in page using socket.io to relay credentials and session tokens to the actor (T1557, T1583.006).
- The kit exposed itself: a code comment references swapping in a grant endpoint, and the badge reads "Community Charter School." A school/grant phishing kit was repurposed for a financial lure with placeholders left in, the branding never matched the sender.
- Pivoting surfaced related low-confidence infrastructure: accessdocuments[.]us, accountsv3slgnin-identifier-continue[.]com, adobeonlinereader[.]org, docsngdocumm[.]com, getmailsg[.]com, securepreesserrve[.]com, yah-signrev[.]info.

item.title: Contagious Interview steps outside the developer workflow
item.description:
DPRK Contagious Interview expands beyond developer bait: 14 trojanized macOS apps impersonating tools like The Unarchiver, Sketch, and Bartender deliver OtterCookie via a four-stage chain.
Key findings:
- Unsigned DMGs and PKGs impersonate popular Mac apps. CFBundleExecutable in Info.plist is hijacked to point to a hidden .macos file compiled via Bunster (shell-to-Go). Gatekeeper blocks execution, so the quarantine xattr must be manually stripped, suggesting targeted delivery where victims are coached through the bypass.
- The four-stage chain: .macos curls /task/mac from 162.0.239[.]85, which fetches tokenlinux.sh, which pulls Node.js and a malicious parser.js. Staging now uses the hidden ~/.task directory. Every retrieval URL beyond the first carries a signed HS256 JWT embedding victim IP, sessionId, step counter, and timestamps.
- Final payload is OtterCookie: a Socket.IO RAT, browser and crypto wallet credential stealer, in-memory filesystem scanner, and clipboard clipper using pbpaste.
- Infrastructure: staging on 162.0.239[.]85:3000, OtterCookie C2 on 147.124.202[.]205 across ports 7671, 7676, 7679. Associated domains include w3pi[.]social, softcus[.]net, and pobelstudio[.]com.
Hunt for unsigned apps with modified Info.plist executables, outbound HTTP to port 3000, Node.js spawned from unexpected parents, and ~/.task directory creation.

item.title: One Blank Field Bypasses Direct Send Control
item.description:
A single empty SMTP envelope field bypasses RejectDirectSend in Microsoft 365, letting unauthenticated senders spoof internal addresses with no credentials, no lookalike domain, and no infrastructure.
- RejectDirectSend evaluates the domain in the SMTP MAIL FROM field, but an empty value (MAIL FROM:<>) gives it nothing to check. ReliaQuest confirmed this in a controlled tenant: the baseline message with an accepted-domain envelope sender was rejected with 550 5.7.68, while the empty-sender message was accepted and queued, headers showing spf=none, dkim=none, dmarc=fail action=oreject, SCL 9, and delivery to Junk. Junk delivery is not a win: the bypass already succeeded before antispam ran.
- Active phishing use from September 2025 through August 2026 across multiple orgs, targeting executives, finance, and procurement with file-sharing and payment lures, several using SVG attachments framed as voicemails. Most messages reached inboxes via filtering exceptions on impersonated addresses, not inbox placement by default.
- IP-restricted inbound connectors blocked every Direct Send attempt regardless of envelope sender in testing. This is the structural fix. RejectDirectSend alone is not sufficient.
Hunt for messages where the envelope Return-Path is empty and the header From uses an accepted internal domain, cross-reference against SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures and any override that let them deliver.

item.title: How Attackers Learn Your Network Before They Attack It
item.description:
Zeek's bro-simple-scan exposes how failed TCP connections betray reconnaissance, and why encoding network knowledge beats pure threshold counting for catching patient adversaries.
- bro-simple-scan watches Zeek connection history strings, S (SYN with no response) and Sr (SYN plus RST), counting unique victim/port pairs per source. At 25 failures it fires one of three notices: Scan::Address_Scan (one source, many hosts), Scan::Port_Scan (one source, one host, many ports), or Scan::Random_Scan (scattered pattern). Darknet integration via bro-is-darknet drops the threshold to 10 when a source touches unused address space, and a separate knock-knock rule fires at 20 unique hosts on a single port (3 if darknet).
- The structural blind spot is slow and distributed scanning. State ages out after 15 minutes by default, so a scanner pacing below two probes per half hour never accumulates enough failures. Split across 50 sources, no single source trips a per-source threshold even when the aggregate pattern is obvious.
- Profile-based detection is the upgrade path. A SYN to a port no host in your network legitimately serves is high-confidence at count one. Zeek already logs every connection; building a baseline of which hosts serve which ports, and who talks to whom, inverts the detection question from "has this source failed enough?" to "does this connection make sense?"

item.title: Chamilo LMS... It's raining 0days, hallelujah, it's raining 0days
item.description:
Chamilo LMS 1.11.36 has 11 zero-days including a fully weaponized pre-auth RCE chain. Schools and enterprises running this widely deployed open-source LMS are exposed to complete server compromise with no credentials required.
Key findings:
- The pre-auth RCE chain starts with CVE-2026-61600, an unauthenticated boolean-based blind SQLi in main/inc/ajax/model.ajax.php via the groupOp field of the JSON filters parameter. An attacker needs only a valid cidReq course code (enumerable from the home page) to dump the admin row including the confirmation_token field, enabling a full password reset without ever touching the admin's mailbox.
- A second pre-auth primitive (no CVE assigned separately) allows unauthenticated POST requests to main/inc/ajax/user_manager.ajax.php with action update_users, overwriting the email of any user including admin (user_id=1). Chained with the password reset flow this gives complete account takeover. The admin row can be restored post-exploit to minimize detection.
- CVE-2026-70647 is an unsafe deserialization in the course backup import feature. course_info.dat inside the ZIP is base64-encoded serialized PHP. An attacker modifies a Document object's path property to coiffeur.php in the web root, re-packages the ZIP, and imports it via the legitimate course import UI. Chamilo trusts the tampered metadata and writes the webshell to /app/courses/{course_code}/coiffeur.php.

item.title: Attackers Actively Exploiting Critical Vulnerability in Elementor Pro Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-32475 (CVSS 9.8) in Elementor Pro is actively exploited, letting unauthenticated attackers upload PHP webshells and take over any WordPress site running the vulnerable plugin across 6 million active installs.
- CVE-2026-32475 hits Elementor Pro <= 4.2.1 via a validation logic flaw in Upload::validation(). Submitting a file upload field as an array where index [0] has an empty filename triggers UPLOAD_ERR_NO_FILE, which causes a premature 'return' instead of 'continue', killing all extension and MIME checks for every subsequent array element. Index [1] then delivers a .php webshell unchallenged, no authentication required.
- The dropped file lands in wp-content/uploads/elementor/forms/ under a randomized name with the attacker-supplied .php extension. That directory should never contain PHP files: its presence is your primary IOC. The webshell observed chains system, passthru, shell_exec, exec, proc_open, and popen for maximum exec compatibility.
- Exploitation began the same day of public disclosure, August 19th, 2026. Over 190,000 attempts blocked. Top attacking IPs include 185.196.220[.]85, 103.84.230[.]85, 103.90.148[.]202, and 216.126.225[.]208.
Hunt your access logs for POST requests to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with action=elementor_pro_forms_send_form, then scan wp-content/uploads/elementor/forms/ for any .php file. Patch to 4.2.2 immediately.

item.title: Gaming the system: how a Chinese-speaking actor turned Brazilian government sites into an SEO weapon
item.description:
Gambling Goblin, a Chinese-speaking cluster linked to Earth Berberoka, has compromised Brazilian 🇧🇷 government .gov.br servers since mid-2025, weaponizing their search reputation for gambling SEO fraud while deploying espionage-grade Linux tooling.

They reverse-proxy specific URL prefixes (/wps, /bmw, /card) to attacker infrastructure while stripping CSP headers so injected gambling content runs freely. A second module uses RC4-decrypted config for selective content injection, consistent with SEO cloaking (T1505.004).
- The Linux toolkit is broad: DownPro (Go downloader, AES-GCM encrypted URLs) drops payloads to paths like /usr/local/bin/systemd-udevd or /tmp/php_sess_<32hex>. oRAT persists as systemd service xtables-addons and hides its GUID in /etc/protocols. PasswordHarvester (3snake-based) ptrace-attaches to sshd/sudo/su and exfiltrates RC4-encoded credentials. AlphaAgent backdoor impersonates [kworker/...] or rsyslogd, uses uTLS to mimic Chrome (defeating JA3/JA4), and camouflages C2 traffic as api.google[.]com.
- Infrastructure spans lookalike C2 domains including api.gitlab[.]bet, github[.]la, and rb.aliyuntsl[.]com, with IPs clustered on AWS AS16509, matching prior Earth Berberoka tradecraft. Daily domain generators rotate fresh infrastructure to outpace blocklists.

item.title: Android App RCE via Dynamic Code Loading
item.description:
Android document viewer app achieves RCE by chaining a path traversal in URI handling with dynamic native library loading, letting an attacker write and execute arbitrary code inside the app's sandbox.
Key findings:
- The vulnerable app's handleIntent() passes an attacker-controlled HTTP/HTTPS URI to copyFileFromUri(), which calls Uri.getLastPathSegment() without decoding percent-encoded characters. Supplying a URL like hxxps://192.168.x[.]x/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fdata%2Fdata%2Fcom.mobilehackinglab.documentviewer%2Ffiles%2Fnative-libraries%2Fx86_64%2Flibdocviewer_pro.so causes the traversal to land outside the Downloads folder and write directly into the app's private files/ directory (T1083, T1105).
- loadProLibrary() unconditionally calls System.load() on files/native-libraries/ABI/libdocviewer_pro.so at every launch. An attacker plants a malicious .so compiled with ndk-build; on next app open, the library executes with the app's UID.
- The attack is delivered entirely via a crafted deep-link intent (scheme: file/http/https, mimeType: PDF), requiring no user permissions beyond what the app already holds.
Takeaway: When reviewing Android apps, flag any combination of getLastPathSegment() feeding a file write path and System.load() referencing that same path. Check AndroidManifest.xml for exported Activities accepting deep links, then trace URI handling through to any file-write or library-load call. Full exploit chain is documented in the write-up.

item.title: Hiding a Signup Button Isn’t Security: From Client-Side Controls to Cross-Tenant Data Exposure
item.description:
A hidden signup button and a client-side feature flag masked a full attack chain: unauthenticated account creation, email verification bypass, self-service privilege escalation, and cross-tenant API key exposure.
Key findings:
- The app set USER_SIGNUP: false in frontend JavaScript but never enforced the restriction server-side. POST /people/ accepted registration requests directly, and the 201 response included the confirm_token needed for verification, handing the attacker the email confirmation secret without inbox access.
- Confirmation bypass used POST /people/password/ with that leaked token to set confirmed: true and receive a valid auth token, skipping the entire email verification step the application was designed to require.
- Mass assignment on PUT /people/{uuid}/ let the newly authenticated user send is_staff: true and receive 200 OK. The backend applied the field with no authorization check, instantly elevating the account.
- With a staff token, GET /people/?domain_uuid= accepted attacker-supplied tenant IDs and returned users from other organizations. GET /domains/ then returned api_keys arrays containing live credentials for multiple tenants.
Takeaway: Hunt your own APIs before attackers do. Replay registration and profile-update requests with Burp, strip the UI entirely, and probe every writable field for mass assignment. Confirm_tokens must never appear in registration responses.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Finds Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability in Gravity Forms
item.description:
CVE-2026-19513 (CVSS 8.1): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in Gravity Forms affects 1M+ WordPress installs, enabling remote code execution on NGINX-backed sites.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-19513, CVSS 8.1 High. Gravity Forms versions up to and including 3.0.2 allow unauthenticated attackers to write a PNG/PHP polyglot to the plugin's public temp upload directory with an attacker-chosen .php extension. The root cause is a cryptographic domain-confusion flaw: wp_hash() was reused without context separation for both public form state and chunk-continuation auth, letting attackers reuse a legitimate URL hash to authenticate a malicious upload continuation request.
- Exploitation requires a public form with a multi-file upload field enabled. PNG and PDF are permitted by default, so no admin allowlist change is needed. The attacker supplies a benign carrier filename (safe.png) while forcing the sanitized temp destination to end in .php, then triggers a final-chunk rename that strips the .part suffix and leaves an executable file on disk.
- Impact is server-dependent. Apache installs are partially mitigated by a .htaccess the plugin writes to the upload directory, blocking PHP execution. NGINX ignores .htaccess, making RCE directly reachable. Even on protected Apache installs, writing a .html file enables stored same-origin XSS.

DllMain triggers the payload chain, which reads an AES-encrypted ValleyRAT DLL from either the PeLoader file or libcef.dll's own resources, decrypts it, and loads it directly into process memory.

It injects a watchdog into svchost (with PAGE_NOACCESS then RWX memory), can mark its own process critical to force a BSOD on termination, and keyloggs via DirectInput8 while capturing clipboard contents to disk.

item.title: Operation RepoGhost: Exposing a Russian-Linked Malware Campaign Hiding in GitHub’s Open-Source…
item.description:
Russian-linked Operation RepoGhost has run 52 malicious GitHub repos since Nov 2025, cycling through CountLoader, Nova macOS stealer, and a Go-based infostealer to hit developers, researchers, and crypto users.
Key findings:
- The infection chain abuses scriptrunner.exe (a signed Microsoft App-V binary) to proxy-execute PowerShell (T1218), pull a stager from Pastebin, download main.exe from 172.237.119[.]163:8000, and load an obfuscated .NET assembly (mid4) entirely in memory. C2 is 194.102.104[.]141:22310. No phishing email, no ZIP, no extra prompt: running the fake PoC or tool IS the infection.
- The in-memory .NET payload checks Win32_OperatingSystem MUILanguages for ru-RU and exits if found, a classic self-exclusion pattern supporting Russian 🇷🇺 attribution alongside the use of CountLoader and Nova, both documented in Russian-speaking crimeware ecosystems.
- Repos were boosted via inflated star/fork counts (one fake CVE-2026-41940 PoC had 313 stars, 39 forks) to rank in GitHub and Google searches, making SEO poisoning the discovery mechanism. Earlier payloads pulled NovaStealer from 217.156.122[.]146; CountLoader staged through python3-library-node[.]com and py-installer[.]cc.
Takeaway: Hunt your environment for scriptrunner.exe spawning PowerShell (T1218), memory-only .NET assemblies, and outbound connections to 194.102.104[.]141:22310. Use ExtremeDumper on suspicious Go processes to recover injected assemblies.

item.title: TerminalFix campaign deploys a reverse tunnel through multistage intrusion
item.description:
TerminalFix, a ClickFix variant, chains DLL sideloading, steganography, and a custom Python reverse tunnel into a full network pivot. Microsoft Threat Intelligence warns affected hosts should be treated as compromised network gateways.
Key details:
- Initial access via fake Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA on compromised sites pastes a PowerShell command that downloads verify_pkg.zip (SHA-256: 18c2090e...8b278f) to C:\ProgramData, then sideloads malicious dui70.dll through the legitimate signed binary LockScreenContentServer.exe (T1574.002). The DLL decodes its next stage entirely in memory.
- Steganography stage (T1027.003) pulls PNG images from bestsocialmedianewspapper[.]com and offlineupdater[.]com, reads RGBA pixel channels to reconstruct executables, then deletes the source images to reduce forensic artifacts.
- Persistence via HKCU Run key and a 60-minute scheduled task, both named LockScreenContentServer_MuODG5yBM (T1547.001, T1053.005). The payload directory is hidden with attrib +h +s (T1564.001).
- Reconnaissance covers nltest domain trusts, net group "domain admins", ADSI user/computer sweeps with multilingual systeminfo, and ping sweeps targeting DC, SQL, backup, and mail server names, classic pre-ransomware triage.
- Python 3.14.5 runtime is dropped and client.py launches via pythonw.exe (no window) to establish a TLS WebSocket reverse tunnel to gitnow[.]dev:443, enabling SOCKS-style TCP proxy access into the internal network (T1572).

item.title: The AI Attack Surface: How Threat Actors Abuse Trusted AI Platforms
item.description:
Threat actors are abusing legitimate AI platforms including Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok as malware delivery channels, hitting 29+ organizations via SEO poisoning, sponsored search, and shared conversations hosted on trusted domains.
Key findings:
- FakeAgent campaign: users searching Bing for the Claude desktop app landed on a malicious Claude Artifact at claude.ai, visually impersonating a legitimate download page. The fake installer redirected to downloading-api.it[.]com and dropped SectopRAT. Incidents continued through August even after the artifact was removed.
- A fake "Apple Support install guide" was hosted on a real claude.ai/share URL and surfaced via a sponsored Google result. Victims pasted a curl command into Terminal, triggering a six-stage MacSync stealer kill chain that harvested cookies, credentials, keychain secrets, SSH keys, and Telegram sessions.
- ChatGPT and Grok shared conversations were SEO-poisoned to rank for queries like "Clear disk space on macOS." The plausible-looking troubleshooting advice delivered ClickFix-style Terminal commands that installed the AMOS stealer. A separate August variant used a fake OpenAI Codex download with the same TTPs.
- The trust chain is the attack: real domains, valid TLS, recognizable branding, and no lookalike URLs mean standard phishing indicators fail to fire.

item.title: TeamPCP Arrests: Two Charged in Australia Over the Supply Chain Campaign That Hit 1,000+ Organizations
item.description:

- TeamPCP (also tracked as UNC6780, PCPcat, ShellForce, DeadCatx3) exploited a privileged token surviving an incomplete rotation in Trivy's GitHub Actions workflows, then published poisoned Trivy releases that flowed into LiteLLM's build pipeline. Two malicious PyPI packages harvested cloud keys, SSH keys, Kubernetes tokens, database passwords, and AI provider credentials. item.title: Russian APT BlueDelta Uses HOOKEDGE to Target Defense and Diplomatic Organizations
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 GRU-linked BlueDelta (APT28) ran a six-month espionage campaign against European government and diplomatic targets using a batch-script backdoor that hides C2 traffic inside Microsoft Edge browsing sessions.
Key details:
- HOOKEDGE is a Windows batch-script backdoor delivered via macro-enabled Word documents with diplomatic lures, including one impersonating Spain 🇪🇸's Ministry of the Presidency timed to a real Spanish-Moldovan meeting ahead of Moldova's September 2025 elections. Targets included government organizations in Romania 🇷🇴, Spain 🇪🇸, and Türkiye from late September 2025 through early April 2026.
- The entire C2 runs through webhook[.]site, a legitimate developer tool. Every 30 minutes a scheduled task pulls a command file via msedge.exe and exfiltrates results to a second webhook endpoint, making traffic indistinguishable from normal enterprise browsing (T1071.001, T1053.005).
- BlueDelta embedded canary tracking pixels named mailopened.jpg and docopened.jpg referencing remote webhook URLs to log exactly when emails were opened, when documents were opened, and when macros executed, giving operators a full phishing funnel analytics view before any payload ran.
- HOOKEDGE shares code, JavaScript variable names, and base64 encoding patterns with the earlier HEADLACE backdoor, confirming evolutionary continuity rather than a new toolset.

item.title: Gryxa: The AI-Built Toolkit That Watches How You Remove It
item.description:
Gryxa, an AI-built RMM abuse toolkit, watches defenders remove it and uploads forensic evidence of the response to the threat actor, across 324 compromised hosts.
Key findings:
- Gryxa uses phishing (invoice_<10digits>.exe) to drop an RMM implant, then builds 7 scheduled tasks in two layers, a permanent WMI event subscription, and a hidden off-path file cache across C:\ProgramData\WinRTCS, .wucache, and .etlcache paths. Any deleted component rebuilds within one minute. Removing the visible RMM client alone does nothing.
- Partial containment starts a clock. When Gryxa loses contact with its relay (wirbe[.]com, seczio[.]com, sevrz[.]com, gryxa[.]com, IPs 144.172.107[.]56 and 209.145.55[.]189), it disables Defender and issues silent uninstall commands against EDR within 10-13 minutes. Defender re-enables once the relay returns, and Defender exclusions it added are never reverted.
- After the RMM implant is removed, a surviving component runs the built-in collect-forensics job: it packages scheduled tasks, event subscriptions, installer logs, process-creation logs, and an RMM inventory, then uploads the archive to actor infrastructure. The attacker reads your response before their next move.
- Credentials from Chromium-based browsers exit via Telegram in plaintext to a single operator account. Around 40 crypto exchange domains are checked for priority; 69 wallet extension IDs are flagged for manual follow-up over the RMM session.
